lines: Scott Kupor, a16z's first employee and now Director of the US Office of Personnel Management, argues the federal workforce's problems are mainly about incentives, not talent: a risk-averse culture rewards avoiding bad headlines over delivering results.

He traces a16z's rise from a 2008-crisis startup to its CAA-inspired 'services' model, where a team of functional specialists replaces the lone super-connector partner, and says marketing gave the new firm category-creating narrative control.
Kupor says performance management in government breaks down when about 90% of senior executives are rated in the top tier, leaving no way to reward real high performers.

He calls the demographics an existential talent crisis: only 7% of federal workers are under 30 and nearly half are over 50, so recruiting should pitch high-impact, shorter-term service rather than lifetime employment.

His modernization agenda includes digitizing 400 million paper retirement files stored in a Pennsylvania mine to cut processing from months to days, and adopting 'permissioned risk' that tolerates failure in non-critical operations.
title: Scott Kupor on Building a16z and Rebuilding the Federal Workforce
